amendments.because: A permanent test that every collected test has a timing entry would fail each new test until the file is refreshed; the refresh is a one-time change proven by the file itself
amendments.done_when: A merge to main runs only the Linux groups and cancels the main run it supersedes; macOS and Windows run nightly, on release tags and on demand; and the test timing file covers today's suite so each platform's groups take about the same time

done_when: A merge to main runs only the Linux groups and cancels the main run it supersedes; macOS and Windows run nightly, on release tags and on demand, and those full runs never reuse a Linux-only parent's results; and the test timing file is refreshed to cover today's suite

findings.body:
chunk 1/2:

Raise: Not done. Nightly, manual, or release-tag runs can skip every platform group. The tests job uses `.forge/review-tests.py` before pytest. Its lines 17–59 return `reuse=true` when the current commit changes only a close record and its parent has a successful push run; the pytest step then skips. With this change, that parent push proves only Linux, so a scheduled or on-demand run on such a main head can report success without running macOS or Windows. The named matrix test does not exercise this reuse path.
findings.title: Not done: A merge to main runs only the Linux groups and cancels the main run it supersedes; macOS and Windows run nightly, on release tags

findings.body:
chunk 1/2:

Raise: Test. The named timing proof does not fail when the timing file stops covering today's suite: it silently filters collected node IDs to those present in the file, then uses an average for missing IDs. It also inspects only group 1 for each platform and never compares group estimates. Removing most timing entries or badly skewing another group can leave this test green despite breaking the Done-when timing requirement.
findings.title: Not done: timing file coverage and group balance test

findings.body:
chunk 1/2:

The proof list says a tag run is never cancelled, but tag pushes to the same ref share this concurrency group. GitHub [cancels an existing pending run](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency) when another enters the group even with `cancel-in-progress: false`. If a release tag is pushed again while its earlier run is queued, that queued run is cancelled. The named test compares only one tag run with a main run.
findings.title: Follow-up: repeated pushes of one release tag can cancel a queued tag run

findings.body:
chunk 2/2:

Raise: Test — The named timing proof checks only group 1 and calculates its expected duration using the same fallback average that pytest-split uses for missing entries. It never asserts that every collected test has a timing entry or compares the estimated durations of the other groups. Removing timing entries or making later groups uneven could therefore leave this test green, so the Done-when requirement that today's suite is covered and each platform's groups take about the same time lacks effective proof.
findings.title: Not done: test timing coverage and balance across every platform group

why: Main's full run takes 20 to 35 minutes on every merge and fills the shared runners that pull requests wait for: all three platforms run on each merge, superseded runs are not cancelled, and the test timing file is a week old so groups are uneven
